title: C++ foundations for problem solving
subtitle: Six small steps: values, conditions, vectors, loops, functions and safe indexing. Use C++17 or later. Examples are complete programs; quick checks ask you to predict their output.

sections.title: Values and output
points: `int` holds whole numbers. `long long` gives a larger range.
`1LL` makes this multiplication use long long before the result is assigned.
sections.summary: Choose a type that can hold the largest intermediate result.
sections.analogy: A larger destination box does not help if a smaller box spills before you transfer the contents.
sections.gotcha: `long long total = a * b` can still overflow when both operands are int. Use `1LL * a * b`.

sections.title: Conditions and blocks
points: `&&` means both conditions must be true.
Braces group the statements controlled by an if or loop.
sections.summary: Write each comparison explicitly: `low <= x && x < high`.
sections.analogy: Check both gates: above the lower bound and below the upper bound.
sections.gotcha: `0 < x < 10` does not test a range in C++. Use `0 < x && x < 10`.

sections.title: A growable list: vector
points: `push_back(x)` adds an item at the end; `back()` reads the last item.
`pop_back()` removes the last item and returns nothing. End operations are amortized O(1) for push and O(1) for pop.
sections.summary: Use vector for ordered values you want to access by index.
sections.analogy: Numbered boxes in a row. An index selects one box directly.
sections.gotcha: Check `empty()` before `back()` or `pop_back()`. Removing the front shifts remaining values and costs O(n).

sections.title: Visit values or indexes
points: A range loop visits each value.
Use `for (int i = 0; i < static_cast<int>(nums.size()); ++i)` when you need the index.
sections.summary: Choose a value loop unless the algorithm needs positions.
sections.analogy: You can inspect every book, or track each book's shelf number when positions matter.
sections.gotcha: `for (int value : nums)` copies each value. Use `int& value` if changes must update the vector.

sections.title: Functions and references
points: `const std::vector<int>&` reads the caller's vector without copying it.
Use `std::vector<int>&` when the function intentionally changes the caller's vector.
sections.summary: State whether a function reads, copies or changes its input.
sections.analogy: A reference borrows the original notebook. A value parameter gets a copy.
sections.gotcha: Passing a large vector by value costs O(n) time and space for the copy. Do not return a reference to a local variable.

sections.title: Empty input and index bounds
points: Valid indexes go from 0 through size minus 1.
Check empty input before accessing the first or last value.
sections.summary: Trace an empty input, a single value and the last valid index.
sections.analogy: Before opening box zero, check that there are any boxes.
sections.gotcha: `nums[nums.size()]` is out of bounds. `operator[]` does not check bounds; invalid access has undefined behavior.

exercises.explanation: 1LL promotes the multiplication to long long, which can hold 3 billion.

exercises.code:
#include <iostream>
int main() { int x = 12; std::cout << (0 < x && x < 10); }
exercises.explanation: 12 is not less than 10. By default cout prints false as 0.
After removing 4, the vector is {3, 1}. Its last value is 1.
The reference x changes each element in the original vector.
The function changes a copy. An int& parameter would change the caller's value.
The empty check prevents an invalid access to v[0].
